title: The Carbon Cycle and Earth Systems
seo_title: Carbon Cycle Worksheets: Reservoirs, Carbon Budget, Keeling Curve and Ocean pH (Earth Science)
standard_text: Develop a quantitative model to describe the cycling of carbon among the hydrosphere, atmosphere, geosphere, and biosphere. Use a computational representation to illustrate the relationships among Earth systems and how those relationships are being modified due to human activity.
meta_desc: Free high school Earth and space science worksheets on the carbon cycle (NGSS HS-ESS2-6, HS-ESS3-6): carbon reservoirs and flows, the yearly carbon budget, the Keeling curve and ocean acidification. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: Carbon cycles through all four spheres.
key_sub: Humans move fossil carbon into the air; the ocean and land absorb only part of it.
body_html:
How to think about it

Carbon moves among the air, oceans, rocks and living things.

  • Reservoirs: rocks and the deep ocean hold the most; the air holds relatively little, so small changes matter.
  • Humans move carbon from fossil fuels (geosphere) to the air. About half stays in the air; the ocean and land take up the rest.
  • Budget: emissions − ocean uptake − land uptake = carbon added to the air (2.1 billion tons ≈ 1 ppm). Extra CO₂ also lowers ocean pH.
Example

Emit 10, ocean 2.5, land 3. Left in air?

10 − 2.5 − 3

Answer: 4.5 billion tons

Example

4.2 billion tons added. ppm rise?

4.2 ÷ 2.1

Answer: about 2 ppm

Common mistakes

  • Thinking most carbon is in the air.
  • Thinking all emitted CO₂ stays in the air.
  • Thinking a lower pH means less acidic.

faq.q: Where is carbon stored on Earth?
faq.a: In rocks (the largest store), the ocean, soils, living things, fossil fuels and the atmosphere.

faq.q: How do humans change the carbon cycle?
faq.a: Burning fossil fuels and clearing forests move carbon into the atmosphere much faster than natural processes remove it.
When seawater absorbs CO₂, it forms carbonic acid, which lowers the ocean's pH and makes it harder for shell-building organisms.

items.q: CO₂ dissolves in seawater and forms carbonic acid. What happens to ocean pH?
c: It goes down (the water becomes more acidic).
items.e: More H⁺ ions → lower pH. Since 1750, surface ocean pH fell from about 8.2 to 8.1.
